To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) grating induction magnitude is a monotonic function of test field height and spatial frequency; and (2) the effect of blurring of inducing/test field boundary is to increase the magnitude of the grating contrast.

(1) the effect of blurring of an inducing/test field edge on the magnitude of the grating inductions produced by that edge is to increase the magnitude of those inductions, and (2) the effect of edge blurring is to produce a small, but significant, elevation in grating induction magnitudes.
(1) grating induction magnitude increases monotonically with decreasing spatial frequency and with increasing test field size and (2) grating induction is not affected by the presence of edge blur.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of high spatial frequency information in the perception of brightness.
the visual induction effect, a brightness phenomenon in which the brightness of a test field is affected by the brightness of an adjacent field.
the visual mechanisms underlying the brightness induction effects produced by the presence of an adjacent test field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the grating induction phenomenon is not a high spatial frequency effect.
the grating induction mechanism is a global one, which operates on the entire inducing/test field, and is not edge-dependent.

the grating induction phenomenon is a brightness induction effect, and that the magnitude of the grating inductions produced are a function of the spatial frequency of the inducing/test edge, but not the spatial frequency of that edge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

grating induction magnitude is determined largely by the spatial frequency content of the inducing/test fields, and is relatively independent of the spatial frequency content or sharpness of the boundary which separates them.
, although the induction effect is mediated by a spatially non-specific mechanism, the magnitude of the effect is determined, at least in part, by spatial frequency and edge information.

grating induction magnitude is a function of test field height and spatial frequency, and that the effect of edge sharpening is small and relatively invariant with test field height and/or spatial frequency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
grating induction magnitude is not a simple function of the luminance of the test field.
grating induction magnitude is relatively insensitive to edge blur and, therefore, is likely mediated by low spatial frequency channels.
the grating induction magnitude is relatively robust against changes in the inducing stimulus.
